"Creating an index through:
index = Index(
	fields=['-name'],
	name='idx'
)
Will generate the valid but not so pretty CREATE INDEX statement: 
CREATE INDEX "idx" ON "schema_author" ("name"DESC)
The following would be expected:
CREATE INDEX "idx" ON "schema_author" ("name" DESC)
This was partially fixed for indexes using opclasses in https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/30903#ticket but it introduced a new quirk when opclasses is used without explicit ordering:
index = Index(
	fields=['name'],
	name='idx'
	opclasses=['text_pattern_ops']
)
Will result in:
CREATE INDEX "idx" ON "schema_author" (“name” text_pattern_ops )
Note the whitespace after text_pattern_ops. When used with a descending order it will look correct. 
Unfortunately in the fix in #30903 it was assumed that the col_suffixes passed to django.db.backends.ddl_references.Columns would be empty for ascending order but instead it will contain empty strings and thus causing this bug. See: https://github.com/django/django/blob/master/django/db/backends/ddl_references.py#L87

CREATE INDEX

An `ExpressionWrapper` delegates its SQL compilation and expression introspection to its wrapped inner expression. Defining `get_group_by_cols` on `ExpressionWrapper` to delegate to `self.expression.get_group_by_cols` ensures that constant expressions (such as `Value`) correctly return an empty list of grouping columns instead of falling back to `BaseExpression.get_group_by_cols`.

    def get_group_by_cols(self, alias=None):

An instance of `Table` was being passed as the `table` argument to `self._index_columns()` in `_create_unique_sql()`, which forwarded it to `Columns(table, ...)`. Because `Columns.references_column()` checks `self.table == table` against a table name string, having a `Table` instance caused `references_column()` (and column reference renaming) to always fail.

Passing `model._meta.db_table` ensures `Columns` receives the table name string, matching how `IndexName` and `Expressions` are constructed.
